newsitem.title: USA: Prosecutor seeks mistrial in Kevorkian case.
newsitem.headline: Prosecutor seeks mistrial in Kevorkian case.

text.p: The prosecutor in Jack Kevorkian's fourth assisted suicide trial asked a judge to declare a mistrial on Thursday, arguing the opening statement by the retired pathologist's lawyer tainted the jury.

Ionia County Prosecutor Raymond Voet said the jury may not be able render a fair verdict after defence attorney Geoffrey Fieger in his openeing statement on Wednesday accused Voet of running a "witch hunt" against Kevorkian.

Judge Charles Miel called a recess to consider the mistrial request, which could lead to charges being dropped against Kevorkian because of double jeopardy laws that prohibit defendants from being tried twice for the same crime.

Kevorkian faced four felony counts for his involvement in the Aug. 30 death of Loretta Peabody, including violating unwritten Michigan "common law" banning assisted suicide and practicing medicine without a license. Peabody, 54, suffered from multiple sclerosis.

Voet on Thursday objected to placards that Fieger showed to the jury, to Fieger's assertion that there is no law against assisted suicide and to his assertions that Voet and other prosecutors were involved in a criminal conspiracy to harass Kevorkian.

"This is the most outrageous slinging of mud I've ever seen," Voet said. "It puts me in the position of having to be a witness. It is simply not fair, your honour, and it went on and on and on yesterday."
Fieger argued on Thursday that there was nothing wrong with his statement and noted he did not object when jurors had to pass a gauntlet of demonstrators against Kevorkian.

"It's okay if we have people demonstrating calling Kevorkian a killer in front of the jury, but it's not okay for Mr. Fieger to come into court to tell the truth and say that he intends to prove that you changed evidence, that you engaged in a conspiracy that you've been harassing the family and this a joke trial for your own political ends," Fieger said.

Peabody, an Ionia resident, was originally thought to have died of natural causes and her body was cremated. But prosecutors began investigating her death after she showed up in a videotape of a consultation with Kevorkian, in which she pleaded for him to help end her suffering.
Voet has acknowledged that her death certificate was changed to show that her death was no longer natural, even though there was no autopsy or examination by the local coroner.
Kevorkian, who has admitted attending 45 deaths since 1990, has been acquitted of assisted suicide charge in three previous trials, once in 1994 and twice in 1996.
If convicted of the latest assisted suicide charge, he faced up to five years prison and a $10,000 fine.
